title: ～間に — “while ～ (something happens during that time)”
summary: 間に means that something happens at some point within a period while a continuing state or action lasts. The period is often shown by a ～ている form. It follows a noun-modifying clause: plain form, or noun + の.

patterns.gloss: V-ている + 間に (出かけている間に)
noun + の + 間に (休みの間に)

body.p: Before 間に use a state or ongoing action, mostly in the ～ている form: 母が出かけている間に, 子どもが寝ている間に. After a noun, use の: 休みの間に.
間に stresses that an action takes place and finishes within that period. 母が出かけている間に、部屋を掃除しました means the cleaning was done during her absence. The main verb is usually a single action.
間 (without に) means the main action continues throughout the whole period: 子どもが寝ている間、本を読んでいました (I kept reading the whole time). Use 間に for a one-time action, and 間 for a continuing one.

examples.ja: 母（はは）が出（で）かけている間（あいだ）に、部屋（へや）を掃除（そうじ）しました。
examples.romaji: Haha ga dekakete iru aida ni, heya o sōji shimashita.
examples.tr: While my mother was out, I cleaned the room.
examples.note: 出かけている marks the period.

examples.ja: 電車（でんしゃ）に乗（の）っている間（あいだ）に、本（ほん）を読（よ）んだ。
examples.romaji: Densha ni notte iru aida ni, hon o yonda.
examples.tr: While I was on the train, I read a book.
examples.note: The sentence ends in the plain form (casual).

examples.ja: 子（こ）どもが寝（ね）ている間（あいだ）に、料理（りょうり）を作（つく）った。
examples.romaji: Kodomo ga nete iru aida ni, ryōri o tsukutta.
examples.tr: While the child was sleeping, I made some food.
examples.note: Making use of the free time.

pitfalls: Use ～ている (a continuing state) before 間に. A one-time verb like 出かける alone doesn't show a period: 出かけている間に.
To say the main action lasts the whole time, use 間 without に.
